study.title: Ranks and the process group
study.locator: Minutes 5:15 to 5:20: what torchrun assigns as global and local rank and why a process group is created

focus: Global rank \(r\) with \(0 \le r < W\) names one process in a run of \(W\) processes. Local rank names the same process inside its node. World size \(W\) is the process count, not the GPU count.
`RANK`, `WORLD_SIZE` and `LOCAL_RANK` come from the launcher. `MASTER_ADDR` and `MASTER_PORT` tell every process where rank 0 waits for the handshake.
Plan one process per GPU and set the device from the local rank, as in `torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)`. Two ranks sharing one GPU serialize kernels and break the one-device-per-rank NCCL setup.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map 2 nodes with 4 GPUs each under one launcher job of 8 processes: the world size, the global ranks on each node, each rank's local rank, and the device each rank sets. Then state which rank holds local rank value 1 on the second node.
traps: Reading local rank as global rank on the second node. Local ranks restart at 0 on each node.
Launching more processes than GPUs and assigning two ranks to one device. NCCL expects one device per rank.
Setting WORLD_SIZE to a value that disagrees with the spawned process count. The init handshake waits for processes that never arrive.

selfTest.q: Two nodes hold 4 GPUs each and one job launches 8 processes. Which global ranks sit on node 1, and what is the local rank of global rank 6?
selfTest.a: Node 1 holds global ranks 4 to 7. Rank 6 has local rank 2 and uses the third GPU of that node.

selfTest.q: What does dist.init_process_group exchange between processes?
selfTest.a: Only handshake locations through the master address and port, a shared file, or a TCP endpoint. No tensors move; setup only makes later communication possible.

selfTest.q: A snippet calls dist.all_reduce(tensor, dst=0). Why is that wrong?
selfTest.a: dist.all_reduce takes no dst argument, and every rank keeps the reduced result. The dst argument belongs to dist.reduce, whose result is valid only on the root.

selfTest.q: Two ranks share one GPU and both call NCCL collectives. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The one-device-per-rank setup breaks. Kernels from both ranks serialize on the shared device, and the communicator is built per device, so sharing is unsupported even when it appears to start.

study.title: Steps 1 to 3 with diffs and the Part 1 video
study.locator: step2_process_group_manager and step3_dataloader with their diffs and the Part 1 video on the model, the process group manager and the dataloader
study.depth: Rebuild the rank grid yourself before reading the solution.

focus: A store is a key-value handshake, either `TCPStore` or `FileStore`. The launcher starts the processes, rendezvous introduces them, and `dist.init_process_group` builds the world group.
The default group holds all \(W\) ranks. `dist.new_group` carves named subsets, one rank may belong to several groups at once, and each group orders its own collectives.
Picotron lays ranks out as `torch.arange(world).view(dp, pp, cp, tp)` and enumerates one subgroup per axis. Every rank must build the identical grid or the groups disagree silently.
File init needs a nonexistent or empty shared file with fcntl locking. Mesh shapes must match on all ranks or setup hangs.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, take world size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron axis order: write the tensor-parallel groups and the data-parallel groups as rank sets.
traps: Reusing one fixed MASTER_PORT for several concurrent runs. The second job fails or joins the wrong rendezvous, so use a distinct port per run.
Trusting a LOCAL_RANK fallback of the form `global_rank % world_size` in example code on multiple nodes. It is not the true node-local rank.
Assuming subgroups inherit a barrier or an ordering from the world group. Each group needs its own calls in the same order.

selfTest.q: What does the store do, and when is it no longer needed?
selfTest.a: It exchanges handshake locations so ranks can find each other during init. After the process group is built, collectives use direct links and no longer consult the store.

selfTest.q: World size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron order: which ranks share a tensor-parallel group, and which share a data-parallel group?
selfTest.a: Tensor-parallel groups are {0, 1} and {2, 3}. Data-parallel groups are {0, 2} and {1, 3}.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 of a subgroup calls all_reduce but rank 1 of the same subgroup calls broadcast. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. Every member of a group must issue the same collective sequence, and subgroups do not inherit ordering from the world group.

selfTest.q: Two jobs on one machine share MASTER_PORT. What goes wrong?
selfTest.a: The second job either fails to bind or rendezvous with the wrong peers. Give each run its own port.

study.title: Send, receive and pipeline handoffs
study.locator: Minutes 7:08 to 7:10: send and receive as point-to-point primitives, with the pipeline send at minutes 9:59 to 10:00 as the use case

focus: Every `dist.send` names a dst and every `dist.recv` names a src, with a preallocated buffer of matching shape and dtype on the receiving rank. Blocking calls return after completion; immediates return a `Work` handle that requires `req.wait()`.
After `dist.isend`, writing the sent tensor is undefined until wait. After `dist.irecv`, reading the receive buffer is undefined until wait. After wait, the transfer is guaranteed.
Broadcast copies one source tensor to all ranks. Reduce combines every rank into dst only, so other ranks hold stale data after the call.
A send with no matching receive, or a receive with no send, blocks forever. The matched pair is the unit that must agree.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two-process exchange: rank 0 builds a 3-element tensor and sends it to rank 1 with isend and irecv plus wait, then rank 1 broadcasts it back so both ranks hold it. State every buffer each rank allocates.
traps: Allocating the receive buffer with the wrong shape or dtype. The call may hang or corrupt instead of raising.
Reading a reduce result on a non-root rank. Only dst holds the combined value.
Reusing a send buffer right after isend without wait. The transfer may still be in flight.

selfTest.q: What is the observable difference between dist.send with dist.recv and dist.isend with dist.irecv?
selfTest.a: The blocking pair returns after the transfer completes. The immediate pair returns a Work handle at once, and the transfer is only guaranteed after req.wait().

selfTest.q: Rank 0 calls isend on a tensor, then overwrites the tensor before wait. Rank 1 receives after its own wait. What can rank 1 hold?
selfTest.a: Anything, including a mix of old and new values. Writing a sent buffer before wait is undefined behaviour.

selfTest.q: Four ranks call dist.reduce with dst 0 and SUM. Afterwards rank 2 reads its tensor. What does it see?
selfTest.a: Its own stale input. Only rank 0 holds the combined sum after a reduce.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 sends to rank 1, but rank 1 never posts a receive and instead calls all_reduce. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. The send waits for a matching receive that never comes, and rank 1 waits at a collective rank 0 never joins.

study.title: Ring costs for all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce
study.locator: Section 8.1, Communication Primitives (pp. 40 to 41): the ring all-gather, ring reduce-scatter and ring all-reduce costs in the rendered equations

focus: Ring all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. With \(N\) ranks and payload \(S\), each half moves \(\frac{N-1}{N} S\) bytes per rank, so all-reduce moves \(2 \frac{N-1}{N} S\).
Gradient averaging is `dist.all_reduce(param.grad.data, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)` on every rank, then division by the world size. The sum is collective; the division is local.
All-gather takes one tensor per rank and returns a length-\(N\) list on every rank. Reduce-scatter takes a list of per-rank inputs and returns one shard per rank.
The tutorial ring challenge sends full buffers, not chunks. Chunking into \(N\) pieces is what turns its \((N-1) S\) cost into the ring cost above.
units.reproduce: By hand, take 4 ranks and a 1 GB payload: reduce-scatter moves 0.75 GB per rank, all-gather moves 0.75 GB per rank, and ring all-reduce moves 1.5 GB per rank. Then run all three on 4 gloo CPU processes and match every rank against the single-process sums.
traps: Passing one stacked tensor to dist.reduce_scatter. It takes a list of per-rank input tensors and raises a type error otherwise.
Forgetting the division by world size after a SUM all-reduce. Every update then silently uses a learning rate scaled by the worker count.
Treating reduce-scatter as a cheaper drop-in for all-reduce. It returns only one shard per rank; the all-gather half is still owed.

selfTest.q: Four ranks all-reduce a 1 GB gradient buffer. How many payload bytes cross each rank, and how does that compare with a naive full-buffer ring?
selfTest.a: Ring all-reduce moves \(2 \times 3/4 \times 1\) GB = 1.5 GB per rank. A naive ring that forwards full buffers moves \((4-1) \times 1\) GB = 3 GB per rank, twice as much.

selfTest.q: Why does the tutorial divide by size after the all-reduce instead of before it?
selfTest.a: The collective must sum identical-scale local gradients first so every rank holds the same total. Division is then a local rescale on each rank; dividing before would still work arithmetically but the shared pattern is sum collectively, rescale locally.

selfTest.q: Two ranks hold [1, 2, 3, 4] and [10, 20, 30, 40]. What does each rank hold after reduce-scatter with SUM?
selfTest.a: Rank 0 holds [11, 22] and rank 1 holds [33, 44]: chunk 0 and chunk 1 of the elementwise sum.

selfTest.q: All-gather and reduce-scatter each move about half the bytes of all-reduce. When does that factor of 2 fail?
selfTest.a: For small latency-bound messages, where startup cost dominates bytes moved. The factor of 2 holds in the bandwidth-bound regime with equal payloads.

study.title: All-to-all meaning and the two-step exchange
study.locator: Minutes 9:57 to 10:00 for the all-to-all meaning, then minutes 19:22 to 19:24 for why one exchange carries counts and a second carries data
study.depth: Watch the semantics segments only. Skip the expert-parallel implementation around them; it belongs to the MoE section.

focus: All-to-all takes a list of per-destination inputs on each rank. Rank \(r\) receives chunk \(r\) from every source, concatenated in source-rank order, so each rank ends with a different mix.
All-reduce gives every rank the same aggregate. All-to-all gives each rank a different slice. Token routing needs the second pattern.
All-to-all fan-out grows as \(O(N^2)\) logical pairs, so contention bounds it where per-node bytes bound all-reduce. Small routed messages are latency-bound.
The gloo backend runs `dist.all_to_all` on CPU in PyTorch 2.14, although the backends table marks it unsupported. Test it instead of routing around it.
units.reproduce: By hand, take rank inputs [[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8]]: rank 0 receives [1, 2, 5, 6] and rank 1 receives [3, 4, 7, 8]. Then run dist.all_to_all on 2 gloo CPU processes and match both ranks.
traps: Assuming all-to-all concatenates like all-gather. All-gather gives every rank the same concatenation; all-to-all gives each rank its own chunk from each source.
Passing single tensors instead of per-rank lists. Both the input and the output of dist.all_to_all are lists with one entry per rank.
Planning uneven token splits without padding. Equal-size chunks are the CPU contract; ragged routing needs explicit padding or a dedicated layout later.

selfTest.q: Two ranks hold [1, 2, 3, 4] and [5, 6, 7, 8]. What does each rank hold after all-to-all?
selfTest.a: Rank 0 holds [1, 2, 5, 6] and rank 1 holds [3, 4, 7, 8]: chunk 0 from each source lands on rank 0, chunk 1 on rank 1.

selfTest.q: Why does expert routing use all-to-all rather than all-reduce?
selfTest.a: Each token must reach one specific expert rank, so destinations need distinct payloads. All-reduce would give every rank the same sum, which cannot route.

selfTest.q: Why is all-to-all contention-sensitive while ring all-reduce keeps constant per-node bytes?
selfTest.a: All-to-all opens a logical pair per rank pair, so pairs grow quadratically while all-reduce only talks to ring neighbours with constant bytes per node.

selfTest.q: The backends table marks gloo all-to-all unsupported. What should you do on CPU in PyTorch 2.14?
selfTest.a: Run it anyway. A 4-process gloo run of dist.all_to_all passes on 2.14.1, so the table entry is stale for CPU.

study.title: Barrier as a rendezvous point
study.locator: Minutes 13:17 to 13:19: all devices wait until every rank arrives at the barrier

focus: Every rank in a group must invoke the same collectives in the same order with agreeing shapes and dtypes. Any deviation hangs or corrupts, because there is no central scheduler to reconcile the calls.
`dist.barrier` blocks until all ranks in the group arrive. It synchronizes arrival only; it moves no tensors and fixes no data skew.

Conditional collectives, where only some ranks enter the call, are the classic hang. So are swapped orders, such as rank 0 calling all-reduce then broadcast while rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce.
`dist.monitored_barrier` with a short timeout plus `TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_DEBUG=DETAIL` names the rank that never arrived. The default 30-minute gloo timeout turns every hang into a long silence.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the order-swap drill on 2 gloo CPU processes with a 20-second timeout: rank 0 calls all-reduce then broadcast while rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce. Predict the timeout, then fix the order and show both calls pass.
traps: Using a barrier as if it synchronizes data. Ranks can arrive together and still hold different tensors.
Running hang drills with the default timeout. Set a timeout of seconds for drills; the 30-minute default is for production patience, not debugging.
Blaming the network for a shape mismatch hang. Agree shapes and dtypes first, then suspect links.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 calls all-reduce then broadcast; rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce with matching shapes. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. Rank 0 waits for a broadcast partner while rank 1 waits for an all-reduce partner, and neither call can complete.

selfTest.q: All ranks call dist.barrier and proceed. Does that prove their tensors agree?
selfTest.a: No. The barrier only proves every rank arrived. Tensor agreement needs the right collectives with matching data, not arrival.

selfTest.q: A job hangs at a collective with the default gloo timeout. How long until it fails, and what finds the guilty rank faster?
selfTest.a: About 30 minutes. A short explicit timeout plus monitored_barrier and DETAIL debug output names the rank that never arrived within seconds.

selfTest.q: Only ranks with nonzero loss call all-reduce. Why is that unsafe even when the math looks conditional-safe?
selfTest.a: Collectives are group operations, not local branches. Ranks that skip the call leave the others waiting, so the condition must be reduced to all ranks first or every rank must enter the call.
